judge_assessment.explanation: Both judge observations survive scrutiny, and I checked the figures at the coordinate level rather than by eye. 'Every strip and circle model visibly supports the stated equal-parts diagnosis' is true in every case: Ben's strip really does break into 1, 2 and 3 sixths; Nina's into 3, 2 and 3 eighths; Cal's bar into 2, 3 and 4 ninths; Kim's pizza is cut at 0, 60, 150 and 240 degrees so the wedges are 60, 90, 90 and 120 degrees with the shaded one smallest; Zoe's rectangle is cut at 1, 2.5 and 4.5 out of 8 so the shaded part is the narrowest. The manual items are genuinely manual and the arithmetic (1/4, 1/6, 3/8, 1/4 > 1/6, 8/2 = 4, 9/3 = 3) is right. One defect the judge did not reach: the declared traps on problems 2 and 4 carry "value": 0.33, so the answer key's Common wrong answers block prints 'If they got 0.33' twice on a Grade 2-3 fractions sheet where the child will write 1/3. The grader is told to watch for a number no student will produce.

strengths_to_preserve: The machine/manual boundary is drawn exactly right, and this case should be the reference for it. Problems 3 and 8 — the two that ask for a drawing plus a sentence — are typed "manual" with descs naming what to check, while problems 2, 4, 6 and 7 route the explanation to the WORK SPACE and put the checkable value on the answer line ('Explain Ben's mistake in the work space. Then write the fraction ...'). That phrasing is what makes machine verification honest here, and it is the pattern the shard-wide flag-open-response-as-manual finding is asking for.

The key gives real grading rubrics for the two manual items, including what NOT to accept: 'Do not accept "because there are four pieces" with no mention of size' and 'Do not accept "she counted wrong"'. It also specifies the acceptable drawing ('Accept any four congruent wedges; the cuts do not have to be horizontal and vertical'), which is what lets a non-specialist grade it consistently.

Problem 4 is deliberately built so guessing from the picture fails: the shaded piece is one of the LARGER pieces, so the misconception answer 1/3 is smaller than the truth 3/8, and the key says so ('guessing from the picture will not rescue it'). That makes it a materially harder item than problem 2 rather than a reskin of it.

Problem 1 is a correct model placed first on purpose, so the student has a clean reference case before meeting five broken ones, and the key flags the predictable over-correction ('Students who answer "no" ... are usually looking at the shading, not the part sizes').

root_causes.description: A trap's optional 'value' is the wrong number a student would actually write, and it is printed verbatim to the grader; but SKILL.md only requires it to round-match its own expr, so a rational misconception answer can be declared as a truncated decimal. render_quick_answers._fmt() then prints that decimal. On a fractions worksheet the printed trap therefore does not match the form the answer is written in, which defeats the purpose of the Common wrong answers block.
evidence: verify.json ids 2 and 4: traps[{'expr': '1/3', 'value': 0.33}] — the expr is exact but the printed value is a two-decimal approximation.

answer_key.pdf Common wrong answers: '2. If they got 0.33: counted the 3 unequal pieces as if they were thirds' and '4. If they got 0.33: counted 1 piece out of 3 unequal pieces instead of the equal small parts'.
The same key's solution text writes the misconception correctly as '\emph{Common wrong answer:} $\tfrac{1}{3}$', so the document contradicts itself on the same page.

The verified answers on those same problems render as proper fractions ($\frac{1}{6}$, $\frac{3}{8}$) because their 'expected' is the string '1/6' / '3/8' — so the renderer handles the fraction form correctly whenever it is given one.

improvements.title: Misconception trap prints 0.33 where the student writes 1/3
improvements.proposed_change: State in SKILL.md's trap section that a trap's 'value' must be written in the same form the student writes the answer — a string '1/3' where the answer is a fraction, matching the existing rule for 'expected' — and have verify.py warn (exit 2) when a trap's value is a float while the same problem's 'expected' is a fraction string or Rational. render_quick_answers._fmt() already renders '1/3' as $\frac{1}{3}$, so the Common wrong answers line fixes itself once the JSON carries the right form. For this case, change ids 2 and 4 to "value": "1/3".
improvements.regression_test: Add a case to tests/test_render_quick_answers.py alongside the trap fixtures: a problem with "expected": "1/6" and traps[{'expr': '1/3', 'value': 0.33}] must produce a verify.py exit-2 warning naming the form mismatch, and the same problem with "value": "1/3" must exit 0 and render the Common wrong answers line as $\frac{1}{3}$. Today the float form passes silently and prints '0.33', so both assertions fail.
improvements.expected_impact: The grading aid becomes usable on fraction sheets: a teacher is told to look for 1/3, which is what a child writes, instead of 0.33, which no child on a Grade 2-3 fractions worksheet will ever produce. It also removes the contradiction between the Common wrong answers block and the solution text on the same page.
improvements.risk: The warning must not fire on genuinely decimal domains (money, measurement, estimation), so gate it on the paired 'expected' being a fraction string or Rational rather than on the trap value alone, and keep it at exit 2 so a false positive never blocks a build.

case_summary: The best-designed case in my batch and the one I would hold up as the model for the machine/manual split: two draw-and-explain items typed manual with real rubrics including what not to accept, four find-and-fix items that route the explanation to the work space and the checkable fraction to the answer line, and figures whose coordinates I verified individually — every unequal-parts diagnosis is genuinely visible in the drawing. The single defect is that the traps on problems 2 and 4 declare "value": 0.33, so the key's Common wrong answers block tells a grader to watch for 0.33 on a sheet where the child writes 1/3, contradicting the key's own solution text two inches lower.
